name: Medieval India – Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526 AD): Slave, Khalji & Tughlaq Dynasties

notes.heading: Overview
points: Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526 AD) marked the establishment of Turkish rule in North India
It had five major dynasties, starting with the Slave Dynasty and ending with the Lodi Dynasty
It introduced new administrative, military, and revenue systems in India
Centralized monarchy with Islamic political institutions

notes.heading: Slave Dynasty (1206–1290 AD) – Overview
points: Also called Mamluk Dynasty (slave-origin rulers)
Founded by Qutb-ud-din Aibak in 1206 AD
First dynasty of Delhi Sultanate
Marked beginning of Turkish rule in India
Strong Turkish slave commanders formed ruling elite

notes.heading: Important Rulers – Slave Dynasty
points: Qutb-ud-din Aibak (1206–1210) – founder of Sultanate rule in India
Iltutmish (1211–1236) – consolidated Delhi Sultanate
Razia Sultana (1236–1240) – first and only female Sultan of Delhi
Balban (1266–1287) – strengthened monarchy and nobility control
Weak successors led to decline of dynasty

notes.heading: Qutb-ud-din Aibak
points: Slave of Muhammad Ghori
Founded Delhi Sultanate after Ghori’s death
Built Qutub Minar (started construction)
Known for generosity, called 'Lakh Baksh'
Ruled briefly and died due to accidental horse fall

notes.heading: Iltutmish – Consolidation of Sultanate
points: Real founder of Delhi Sultanate structure
Introduced Iqta system
Completed Qutub Minar
Strengthened central administration
Got recognition from Abbasid Caliph

notes.heading: Razia Sultana
points: First female ruler of Delhi Sultanate
Faced opposition from Turkish nobility (Chahalgani)
Promoted merit-based administration
Ruled only for a short period
Killed in rebellion

notes.heading: Balban
points: Strengthened Sultan’s authority
Introduced theory of kingship (divine right concept)
Repressed nobility (Chahalgani)
Maintained strict law and order
Strengthened military discipline

notes.heading: Slave Dynasty – Administration
points: Iqta system introduced (land revenue assignments)
Military aristocracy dominated administration
Sultan was central authority
Nobility played key role in governance
Revenue collection system was developed

notes.heading: Khalji Dynasty (1290–1320 AD) – Overview
points: Founded by Jalal-ud-din Khalji
Marked expansion of Delhi Sultanate
Known for military campaigns and economic reforms
Alauddin Khalji was the most powerful ruler
End of Turkish monopoly in administration

notes.heading: Alauddin Khalji (1296–1316 AD)
points: Most powerful Khalji ruler
Expanded empire into Gujarat, Rajasthan, Deccan
Defeated Mongol invasions multiple times
Introduced market control reforms
Maintained strong centralized authority

notes.heading: Military Reforms of Alauddin Khalji
points: Large standing army maintained
Chehra (descriptive roll) system introduced
Dagh system (branding of horses)
Direct payment of soldiers in cash
Reduced corruption in military recruitment

notes.heading: Market and Economic Reforms
points: Controlled prices of essential goods
Regulated grain supply system
Strict market inspection system
Fixed prices for soldiers and civilians
Aimed at sustaining large army cheaply

notes.heading: Administrative Features – Khalji
points: Strong centralized monarchy
Reduced power of nobility
Efficient revenue collection system
Direct control over Deccan and North India
Expansion of intelligence network

notes.heading: Tughlaq Dynasty (1320–1414 AD) – Overview
points: Founded by Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq
Known for experiments in administration
Capital shifted from Delhi to Daulatabad (failed experiment)
Faced rebellions and political instability
Marked decline phase of Delhi Sultanate

notes.heading: Important Rulers – Tughlaq Dynasty
points: Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq – founder
Muhammad bin Tughlaq – most controversial ruler
Firoz Shah Tughlaq – focused on administration and welfare
Later rulers were weak
Dynasty weakened by rebellions

notes.heading: Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1325–1351 AD)
points: Known for bold and failed experiments
Shifted capital from Delhi to Daulatabad
Introduced token currency (failed)
Increased taxation in Doab region
Faced multiple rebellions

notes.heading: Firoz Shah Tughlaq
points: Focused on welfare measures
Built canals, rest houses, and cities
Reduced harsh taxation
Encouraged agriculture development
Weakened central authority

notes.heading: Tughlaq Administration
points: Iqta system continued
Strong military initially, later weakened
Decentralization increased over time
Large public works projects
Growing regional autonomy

notes.heading: Decline of Tughlaqs
points: Failed policies of Muhammad bin Tughlaq
Frequent revolts in provinces
Rise of independent regional kingdoms
Weak successors
Invasion by Timur in 1398 weakened Sultanate further

notes.heading: Significance of Delhi Sultanate (Slave, Khalji, Tughlaq)
points: Established Islamic rule in North India
Introduced Persian administrative system
Strengthened centralized monarchy
Developed Indo-Islamic culture
Set foundation for Mughal Empire

name: Medieval India – Sayyid & Lodi Dynasty, Mongol Attacks, Administration & Economy

notes.heading: Overview
points: Sayyid (1414–1451) and Lodi (1451–1526) dynasties were the last phases of the Delhi Sultanate
This period saw political weakening and rise of regional powers
Frequent Mongol invasions and internal conflicts destabilized the Sultanate
Administrative structure continued but became weaker over time
Economy remained agrarian with declining central control

notes.heading: Sayyid Dynasty (1414–1451 AD) – Overview
points: Founded by Khizr Khan after Timur’s invasion (1398)
Ruled Delhi Sultanate in name but had weak control
Considered puppet rulers under Timurid influence
Four rulers in short span of time
Authority limited to Delhi and nearby regions

notes.heading: Important Sayyid Rulers
points: Khizr Khan (founder) – appointed by Timur
Mubarak Shah – tried to stabilize administration
Muhammad Shah – faced internal rebellions
Alam Shah – last ruler, abdicated voluntarily
Dynasty ended in 1451 CE

notes.heading: Features of Sayyid Dynasty
points: Weak central authority
Frequent rebellions by nobles and governors
Limited territorial control
Dependence on powerful nobles
Decline of Sultanate prestige

notes.heading: Lodi Dynasty (1451–1526 AD) – Overview
points: First Afghan (Pashtun) dynasty of Delhi Sultanate
Founded by Bahlul Lodi in 1451
Strengthened Afghan influence in North India
More stable than Sayyid dynasty
Ended with Battle of Panipat (1526) against Babur

notes.heading: Important Lodi Rulers
points: Bahlul Lodi – founder, established Afghan nobility rule
Sikandar Lodi – expanded territory and strengthened administration
Ibrahim Lodi – last Sultan, defeated by Babur
Sikandar Lodi shifted capital to Agra
Ibrahim Lodi faced internal rebellion and weak control

notes.heading: Sikandar Lodi
points: Strong administrative ruler
Promoted trade and agriculture
Founded city of Agra
Controlled Afghan nobles effectively
Encouraged Persian culture and administration

notes.heading: Ibrahim Lodi
points: Last ruler of Delhi Sultanate
Faced rebellion from Afghan nobles
Harsh and unpopular administration
Defeated by Babur in 1526
Death marked end of Delhi Sultanate

notes.heading: Mongol Attacks on India
points: Mongol invasions occurred frequently during Delhi Sultanate period
Led by Mongol tribes from Central Asia
Major invasions during Khalji and Tughlaq periods
Delhi Sultanate resisted most invasions successfully
Mongols failed to establish permanent rule in India

notes.heading: Causes of Mongol Attacks
points: Expansionist policy of Mongol Empire
Weak frontier regions in North-West India
Desire for wealth and territory
Political instability in Central Asia
Strategic importance of Indian subcontinent

notes.heading: Major Mongol Invasions
points: Repeated attacks during Alauddin Khalji’s reign
Mongols reached Delhi region several times
Defeated by strong Khalji military system
Later invasions during Tughlaq period
Timur’s invasion in 1398 severely weakened Sultanate

notes.heading: Impact of Mongol Attacks
points: Strengthened Delhi Sultanate military reforms
Led to large standing armies
Increased fortification of cities
Frequent instability in North-West frontier
Contributed to decline of later Sultanate dynasties

notes.heading: Administration under Sayyid & Lodi
points: Continued Iqta system from earlier Sultanate
Central authority weakened significantly
Nobles (Amirs) became powerful
Governors had semi-independent control
Judicial system based on Sharia and local customs

notes.heading: Lodi Administration
points: More Afghan tribal influence in administration
Sikandar Lodi strengthened central control temporarily
Revenue system based on land assessment
Military supported by Afghan nobles
Capital shifted to Agra for strategic reasons

notes.heading: Iqta System (Continued)
points: Land revenue assigned to nobles in return for service
Gradually became hereditary in later period
Reduced central revenue control
Weakened during Sayyid and Lodi rule
Important feature of Sultanate administration

notes.heading: Military Administration
points: Army mainly composed of cavalry and infantry
Dependence on Afghan tribal forces in Lodi period
Weak central military organization
Frequent rebellions by nobles
Defence against external invasions weakened

notes.heading: Economy under Late Sultanate
points: Agriculture remained primary economic activity
Land revenue was main source of income
Decline in trade and urban prosperity
Local economies became more dominant
Currency system weakened in some regions

notes.heading: Trade and Urban Centres
points: Decline of large urban centers compared to earlier Sultanate
Regional trade continued at local level
Agra emerged as important commercial center
Decline of long-distance trade due to instability
Merchant activity reduced in some regions

notes.heading: Causes of Decline of Sultanate
points: Weak Sayyid rulers with limited authority
Internal rebellions and noble conflicts
Frequent Mongol and Timurid invasions
Rise of regional kingdoms (Bengal, Malwa, Gujarat)
Final defeat by Babur in 1526 CE

notes.heading: Significance of Sayyid and Lodi Period
points: Marked final phase of Delhi Sultanate
Transition towards Mughal rule in India
Rise of Afghan political influence
Shift of power centers to regional kingdoms
End of medieval Sultanate structure

name: Medieval India – Urbanization, Society & Culture, Scientific Knowledge, Legal System & Decline of Delhi Sultanate

notes.heading: Overview
points: Delhi Sultanate period witnessed significant urban growth followed by gradual decline in later phase
Society and culture reflected Indo-Islamic synthesis
Scientific knowledge and legal institutions were influenced by Persian and Islamic traditions
Later Sultanate period saw weakening administration and rise of regional powers
Urbanization was closely linked with trade, administration, and military needs

notes.heading: Urbanization under Delhi Sultanate – Overview
points: Growth of new cities like Delhi, Agra, Daulatabad, and Lahore
Urban centers developed around administration, trade, and military garrisons
Market towns expanded due to trade policies
Craft production and guilds supported urban economy
Urbanization peaked during Khalji and Tughlaq periods

notes.heading: Major Urban Centers
points: Delhi – political capital and administrative hub
Agra – developed under Lodi rulers as important center
Daulatabad – temporary capital under Muhammad bin Tughlaq
Lahore – strategic military and trade center
Multan – key trade and commercial hub

notes.heading: Factors Promoting Urbanization
points: Centralized administration of Delhi Sultanate
Growth of trade routes (both inland and international)
Military garrisons and forts
Royal patronage and court culture
Influx of artisans and merchants from Central Asia

notes.heading: Decline of Urbanization
points: Political instability in late Sultanate period
Frequent invasions (Mongols and Timur)
Decline of long-distance trade
Weak central administration
Rise of regional kingdoms reducing importance of Delhi

notes.heading: Society under Delhi Sultanate
points: Hierarchical society with Sultan at top
Division between ruling elite and common people
Indo-Islamic cultural synthesis developed
Caste system continued among Hindus
New Muslim elite (Turks, Afghans, Persians) emerged

notes.heading: Social Structure
points: Aristocracy dominated political and social life
Ulema (religious scholars) had influence in society
Artisans and merchants formed urban middle class
Peasants formed majority of population
Women had limited political rights but participated in economy

notes.heading: Indo-Islamic Cultural Synthesis
points: Blending of Persian, Turkish, and Indian traditions
Development of Urdu language
Fusion in architecture (Indo-Islamic style)
Music and art influenced by Persian culture
Religious tolerance varied across rulers

notes.heading: Religion and Culture
points: Islam and Hinduism coexisted with interactions
Sufi saints promoted spiritual harmony
Bhakti movement influenced religious thought
Mosques and temples coexisted in urban spaces
Sufi khanqahs became centers of learning

notes.heading: Scientific Knowledge under Sultanate
points: Influence of Persian and Arabic scientific traditions
Advancement in astronomy and medicine
Translation of Sanskrit texts into Persian
Use of mathematics in administration and architecture
Limited indigenous scientific innovation compared to earlier periods

notes.heading: Fields of Knowledge
points: Astronomy – used for calendar and navigation
Medicine – Unani system practiced
Mathematics – used in taxation and architecture
Geography – knowledge expanded through trade routes
History writing developed under royal patronage

notes.heading: Legal System of Delhi Sultanate
points: Based on Sharia (Islamic law) for Muslims
Qazis (judges) administered justice
Hindus followed customary laws in personal matters
Sultan was the highest judicial authority
Blend of Islamic law and local customs

notes.heading: Judicial Administration
points: Qazi-ul-Quzat was chief judicial officer
Local qazis handled regional disputes
Muhtasibs ensured moral and market regulation
Royal courts handled major cases
Justice system was centralized but uneven in practice

notes.heading: Challenges Leading to Decline of Sultanate – Overview
points: Weak successors after powerful rulers
Frequent internal rebellions by nobles
Rise of regional kingdoms (Bengal, Gujarat, Malwa, Deccan)
Continuous Mongol and Timurid invasions
Administrative decentralization and fragmentation

notes.heading: Political Challenges
points: Conflict among nobility (Amirs)
Weak central authority in Sayyid and Lodi periods
Loss of control over distant provinces
Rise of independent regional rulers
Succession disputes weakened stability

notes.heading: Economic Challenges
points: Decline in long-distance trade
Disruption due to invasions
Reduced revenue collection efficiency
Weak currency and market instability
Agricultural distress in some regions

notes.heading: Military Challenges
points: Frequent Mongol invasions
Timur’s invasion (1398) devastated Delhi
Dependence on feudal nobles for army
Weak frontier defense
Internal rebellions by military commanders

notes.heading: Administrative Challenges
points: Iqta system became hereditary
Decline in central control over provinces
Corruption in administration
Weak intelligence and communication systems
Over-dependence on local elites

notes.heading: Significance of Urbanization and Sultanate Decline
points: Urban growth laid foundation for later Mughal cities
Indo-Islamic culture became permanent feature of India
Legal and administrative systems influenced later regimes
Decline of Sultanate paved way for regional kingdoms and Mughal rise
Transition from medieval Sultanate to early modern period
